item.title: 'I'm a hard yes': Hakeem Jeffries announces support for Hegseth impeachment
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) came out in support of impeaching Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on Sunday, telling ABC News he's a "hard yes." "I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe," Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week." "Pete Hegseth has got to go." Asked by "This Week" co-anchor Jonathan Karl if he's confident all House Democrats will join him in supporting the potential resolution, Jeffries said his conference will "have that conversation" on Tuesday morning, when members convene in Washington for the first time since the midterm election. ABC News - House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) appears on ABC News' "This Week." "But I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution," Jeffries said. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, the outgoing Republican lawmaker who has often clashed with President Donald Trump, told ABC News he intends to reintroduce a privileged resolution to impeach Hegseth as early as Monday. By raising a question of privilege on the floor, leaders are required to schedule a vote on it within two legislative days. Ezra Acayan/Pool via Reuters - PHOTO: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth arrives for the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting, October 28, 2026 in Cebu, Philippines. Massie’s resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing the defense secretary of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973, in addition to other alleged offenses. Thus far, Trump has defended Hegseth, telling reporters Thursday that he has “done a fantastic job.” The president also told Karl the same day, “I have every intention to keep him.” Abdul El-Sayed says Democrats will work with Trump if 'he wants to act serious' Hegseth also defended himself Thursday in a video posted on social media. “A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth said. “It's all about the politics of personal destruction — didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me.” ‘Irresponsible’ decision to make Stephen Miller chief of staff Jeffries, who is likely to become the next speaker of the House in January, said Sunday that he has still not spoken to Trump since the midterm elections, which he described as a "tremendous repudiation of MAGA extremism." "The country clearly has had enough. And we got to fight for an affordable America," Jeffries said. "People are drowning in this failed Republican economy. And enough is enough in that regard. That’s why we’re going to fight to lower the high cost of living on all the things. And we have to." Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images - PHOTO: FILE: President Trump Names Stephen Miller As New White House Chief of Staff While Trump told ABC News in a phone interview after the election that he thinks he can work with Democrats, Jeffries questioned the president's intentions, given his decision announced Friday to elevate White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, a longtime Trump loyalist, to the position of White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. "It’s an awful choice. Stephen Miller is the architect of Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine and has unleashed billions of taxpayer dollars to brutalize and kill American citizens, like Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good , and at the same period of time to violently target law-abiding, immigrant families and communities all across the country. So, you know, it was an irresponsible decision in my view," Jeffries said. Trump says chief of staff Susie Wiles out, Stephen Miller will replace her "There’s not going to be an opportunity, certainly, to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents. And we’re committed to forcefully pushing back against the extremism that they may try to continue to unleash on the American people," he added. Karl pressed Jeffries to clarify if he means that he won't be able to communicate with Miller in the way he sometimes communicated with outgoing chief of staff Wiles. "It’s not going to happen with the new chief of staff to the extent that he lacks -- because he clearly represents, along with Pete Hegseth and a few others, a really toxic brand of political engagement, of politics and of governance. And the American people just voted for that kind of MAGA extremism to be eradicated," Jeffries said. Democratic priorities for legislation and investigations Bringing down costs for housing, groceries, gas and healthcare will be top priorities for his party in the new Congress, Jeffries said, as well as ending the war with Iran, stopping "the Trump tariffs," and "[reversing] the Medicaid cuts that put the health insurance of millions of Americans at risk and threatens to close hospitals all over the place." "The American people clearly want change that’s bold, change that’s transformational, and change that is dramatic," Jeffries, said, adding "we certainly need to reverse the SNAP cuts, and we need to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits. And hopefully we’ll see some courage by a few of our colleagues on the other side of the aisle to work on these issues to get things done." 'Safe to say that we are a blue state' Georgia Gov.-elect Bottoms says after Democrats sweep state offices The Democratic Party is "committed to moving aggressively during the first 100 days of the new Congress and beyond to keep our word," said Jeffries. According to ABC News national voter polls, 55% of voters who voted for U.S. House races said that government corruption was "crucial" to their vote; another 36% said it was a "major factor." In a two-word statement released late Tuesday after Democrats were projected to take control of the House, Rep. Robert Garcia, the presumptive chairman of the House Oversight Committee, stated: "Lawyer up." Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks during a press conference in Washington, November 4, 2026. "Well, there’s a cost to corruption. And throughout this campaign we’ve promised that we would focus certainly on affordability and driving down the high cost of living, and on accountability in the face of the unprecedented corruption that we’ve seen unleashed on the American people by the Trump cartel," Jeffries said. "We’re committed to cleaning up the mess wherever it’s found. That’s in Congress, in the Supreme Court and with respect to this administration." Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: President Donald Trump participates in a roundtable in the East Room of the White House in Washington, October 21, 2026, alongside US Attorney General Todd Blanche. For its part, the administration is saying it will investigate Democrats. Trump said Saturday that he ordered the Department of Justice to examine what he deemed "criminal" acts by Democrats, though he did not provide examples to support his allegations. Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday echoed the president's statement. "What we've seen over the past several days and even over the past several weeks are outright threats, many, many by elected members of Congress and some senators against anybody that's conservative and anybody that that happens to be a Republican," Blanche told CNN. "Over the last several days, we've seen it, that rhetoric even rise up to the point where they're already -- before they're even in power, they're already talking about investigations and impeachments with no basis, no facts, just out there running around -- that that should be something that that President Trump is very concerned about. And certainly I am as well." This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/im-hard-hakeem-jeffries-announces-support-hegseth-impeachment/story?id=137952235

item.title: Battle between Congress and Trump looms as he vows political comeback
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The devastating US midterm election loss leaves President Donald Trump politically hamstrung as he enters the last two years of his presidency (Alex WROBLEWSKI) Donald Trump vowed a political comeback Sunday as the major parties clashed over Democrat threats to prosecute top administration officials after the president's Republicans lost control of Congress in midterm elections. The devastating results in last Tuesday's vote leave Trump politically hamstrung as he enters the remaining two-year 'lame duck' period of his White House tenure, while opening the door to multiple investigations by the Democrat-controlled Congress of the president, his family and senior members of his administration. On political talk shows Sunday, incoming congressional leaders from the Democratic Party promised to hold Trump and his aides to account, while the president's top law officer resolved to defend them and Trump dug in his heels on social media. "America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election," Trump said in a post on Truth Social, adding that the stock market that had grown during his tenure took a loss after the vote. "But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!" On Friday, a defiant Trump appointed hardline advisor Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, signaling a bare-knuckle fightback -- even though many Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have reflected on why they had lost so badly at the ballot box. Miller was architect of Trump's tough immigration policy that analysts have identified as a contributing factor to the unpopularity of Republicans. Amid Democrat threats for administration officials to "lawyer up," Trump said Saturday he was ordering the Justice Department to examine Democratic threats to impeach members of his administration, likening it to "extortion." - 'They can come after us' - That stance stoked a war of words between top Republicans and Democrats on the Sunday talk shows. Attorney General Todd Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump and now head of the Justice Department, vowed to actively defend Trump and senior members of his administration. "You have members of Congress who, after Tuesday, have done nothing but threaten everything that's happening in this administration," Blanche told CNN, citing impeachment threats against Miller after his appointment. "If they try to come after Stephen Miller...instead of actually just conducting oversight and leading, of course the Department of Justice will be there to defend him." Robert Garcia, the ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, took aim at Blanche, saying one role of Congress under the US constitution is to hold the executive branch to account. "All he wants to do is protect Donald Trump, is protect Donald Trump's cabinet and administration officials. That is not his job," Garcia told CNN, vowing to stop corruption and investigate "those that are committing crimes against the American public." "They can come after us however they want. We're not going to be intimidated," added Garcia. With control of committees in both chambers of Congress, Democrats can summon officials, demand documents and hold public hearings, putting Trump and his senior aides under intense scrutiny. Likely subjects include the Trump family's business and cryptocurrency dealings, government contracts involving billionaire Elon Musk, cuts to federal agencies, immigration enforcement and the conduct of the Iran war. Hakeem Jeffries, set to become speaker of the new Democrat-controlled House of Representatives, said he would support an effort to oust Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a key architect of the war on Iran that began in February. "I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC, when asked about a Republican lawmaker's reported plan to introduce an impeachment motion as early as Monday. "The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go." During his first presidency, Trump himself was impeached by the House twice, but on both occasions he was acquitted by the Senate. msp/md This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-vows-comeback-bitter-showdown-160116637.html

item.title: 'Trump has cost us': MAGA loyalists question his future after midterm losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Ned Parker, John Shiffman, Mike Spector, Peter Eisler and Linda So DALLAS, Nov 8 (Reuters) - As Republicans faced a nationwide drubbing in Tuesday’s midterm elections, supporters streamed out of a Dallas ballroom where they’d hoped to toast a win for US Senate candidate Ken Paxton, a favorite of President Donald Trump. In the hotel bar, Michael Little, a 59-year-old businessman and three-time Trump voter, stared at the president’s image on a television screen. “People are pissed off at Trump. Trump has cost us,” he said, capturing a sentiment rippling through the president’s Make America Great Again movement after the Republican Party’s worst electoral defeat in decades. Across the coalition, some supporters who once viewed Trump as MAGA’s greatest asset are beginning to question whether he’s become its biggest liability. The midterm losses amounted to more than a repudiation of Trump. They were a referendum on the political and cultural movement he built. A defining ‌force in American politics that began as a campaign slogan during Trump’s 2016 presidential run now faces a potentially existential reckoning after voters disillusioned with soaring fuel prices, the Iran war and Washington corruption delivered Democrats decisive congressional majorities. Trump’s first major response to the midterms came on Friday. Instead of changing course, he doubled down on the movement’s core. He promoted Stephen Miller, the main architect of the administration’s hardline immigration crackdown, to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Wiles was seen ‌as a stabilizing force inside an often chaotic White House. The move was celebrated by some of MAGA’s most ardent influencers, who saw it as a return to the anti-immigration agenda at the movement’s roots. “Exactly the energy we need,” right-wing influencer Benny Johnson posted on X to his 4.1 million followers. “Solid move. It’s Miller Time.” The White House did not directly answer Reuters' questions about why Republicans lost, the defeat of candidates who embraced Trump's false 2020 election claims, or where MAGA goes from here. Instead, it pointed to Trump's remarks on Wednesday, when he said, "If I were on the ballot, we would have won." He also said it was "largely true" that the Iran war had ​cost Republicans because "it drove the gasoline up," but that he’d do it again. For nearly a decade, MAGA has reshaped the Republican Party and transformed national debates on issues such as trade, immigration, race and gender. The movement installed loyalists throughout federal agencies, cracked down on immigration and pressured corporations and public institutions to retreat from diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. MAGA survived the fallout from the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol and propelled Trump back to the White House. In Trump’s second term, MAGA was no longer a faction of the Republican Party; it was the party. Now, the Democrats’ sweeping victory has forced the movement to grapple with an unexpected question: Is MAGA over? Reuters interviews with more than a dozen MAGA activists, influencers, party strategists, Christian nationalist leaders and researchers who track right-wing politics, along with a review of MAGA supporters' posts and podcasts since Tuesday, show a movement turning its anger on itself. The stolen-election claims that have driven MAGA since Democrat Joe Biden beat Trump in the 2020 presidential election have mostly gone quiet. Instead, supporters are blaming Republican leaders and Trump's advisers, and in some cases the president himself, for broken promises on living costs, the Iran war and the government’s decision to redact or withhold major portions of its investigative files on late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. MAGA’s factions also disagree about what comes next. Some want a return to populist and nationalist basics. Some want a movement less tied to one man. And a vocal minority say MAGA is already dead. “We have to rebuild,” Steve Bannon, a prominent MAGA proponent, podcaster and former Trump White House adviser, told Reuters. He urged the party to double down on an aggressive populist and nationalist agenda and praised Trump for elevating Miller. “Miller's appointment ‌as chief of staff underpins my point,” he said. “There is no more hardcore MAGA proponent than Stephen.” As pro-Trump internet forums digested the election results, a notable slice of self-described MAGA loyalists – ⁠more than 20% – raised doubts about the movement’s leadership and direction, according to an analysis of social media traffic done for Reuters by PeakMetrics, a data intelligence firm. About half of that cohort remained supportive of the MAGA movement but no longer backed Trump as its leader. The other half remained loyal to, though critical of, the president himself. The analysis was based on 12,850 posts sampled from a universe of 4.6 million Trump-related comments on X and Reddit from 9 p.m. on Election Day to 8 p.m. the next evening. It found broad concern among MAGA supporters as the results became clear. Of the posts that assigned blame for the rout, nearly a third said concerns about the Iran war and Israel’s influence over US policy had overshadowed Trump’s message. A quarter said Republicans not fully committed to the MAGA agenda had undermined ⁠the movement. The results left Trump facing large Democratic majorities in both chambers of Congress. Democrats could hold as many as 56 of the Senate's 100 seats, more than enough to block his judicial nominees. They will also hold governorships in all seven battleground states Trump won in 2024, and they swept every statewide race in Texas, which last backed a Democrat for president in 1976. Some prominent Republicans, long wary of a MAGA base that punished dissent, have begun openly criticizing Trump. Republican US Senator Ron Johnson of Wisconsin said on Saturday that corruption was present in “all branches of government,” including “I’m sad to say, within the Trump administration.” He cited Calley Means, a former White House adviser who told "The Joe Rogan Experience" podcast on Friday that Trump's top aides catered to special interests and blocked policies popular with Trump’s Make America Healthy Again movement. Voters "were expecting us to drain the swamp, but it seems like the swamp won," Johnson told Fox News. Asked about Johnson's remarks and Means' accusations, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster did not address the corruption allegations, saying Trump had "made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again." On Sunday, Republican US Representative Marlin Stutzman of Indiana, who won reelection despite his party's losses, called Trump’s promotion of ​Miller a “bad mistake.” “You ​don’t promote those who were in charge,” Stutzman told CNN. “He’s not liked out here in the Midwest by people. They don’t like his tone,” he said of Miller. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Miller had "been a key player” in delivering on Trump's agenda “since day one" and would "continue to deliver historic successes" as ​chief of staff. The White House also pointed to statements from 19 Republican lawmakers supporting Miller’s promotion. ‘MAGA IS STALE’ The midterm losses have muffled one of MAGA's loudest refrains: Since Tuesday, talk of election fraud ‌has virtually vanished among right-wing influencers. “I have been banging the drum of rigged and stolen elections since 2020, but that is not why we lost the midterms,” Rogan O’Handley, a MAGA influencer who posts under the name DC_Draino, wrote on X to his 2.3 million followers. “We lost because we failed to fix the things voters sent us to do.” He didn’t respond to a request for comment. After the 2020 election, Trump supporter Isabella DeLuca was among thousands who stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021. She was charged with five crimes, including theft of a table from inside the Capitol, and pleaded not guilty. Her case was dismissed after Trump returned to office and pardoned her. This time, the 26-year-old conservative influencer directed her anger toward what she described as out-of-touch Republican leaders who failed to appeal to Gen Z voters on affordability, avoiding foreign wars and other key issues. “Republicans were just lazy. They felt like that they were entitled to people's votes and that people would vote for them no matter what,” DeLuca told Reuters. “It goes to show you that you do have to earn people's votes, and that even in a super red state like Texas, you're not untouchable.” The MAGA movement this year appeared "tired," she said. That sentiment was echoed in online right-wing forums, said Jennifer Golbeck, a University of Maryland professor who has analyzed MAGA-related posts since 2016. She said engagement by Trump’s most loyal backers has steadily declined since January, including a 27% drop in posts and comments on Patriots.Win, a popular MAGA forum. ”The enthusiasm and the passion even among this hardest core group of supporters hasn't really been there," Golbeck said. "They are saying that ‘MAGA is stale.’ It’s not new and exciting like it once was.” Fox News, a cable network that has long been a key platform for MAGA voices, saw a sharp decline in viewership ahead of the midterms, with its total daytime audience down 27% in October from a year earlier, according to Nielsen, the audience measurement firm. In a statement to Reuters, Fox said it drew more viewers than its cable-news rivals on election night. “FOX News has been the number one network in cable news for a quarter century,” the network said. Some prominent right-wing influencers blamed the president’s advisers ‌or Republican lawmakers – but rarely Trump himself – for ignoring key voter concerns. In posts, online broadcasts and interviews with Reuters, many blamed dissatisfaction with the economy, though they differed on other reasons for Tuesday's results. It wasn't just failure to address affordability that "crushed" Republicans, said Ben Shapiro, co-founder of the conservative ​site Daily Wire, on his online show on Wednesday. “If you’re talking about an electoral catastrophe – a wipeout like we saw last night – you need more ingredients. Here are the other ingredients: chaos and corruption.” Laura Loomer, an influencer close to Trump, wrote on X: “America is over and the American Dream is dead.” Yet she told Reuters the ​losses did not signal the end of MAGA, arguing that anyone seeking the 2028 Republican presidential nomination would need Trump’s base. “The Republican Party belongs to President Trump,” Loomer said. “The MAGA movement is still the majority of the GOP base, and whoever wants to run ​for president in 2028 on the GOP ticket, they would be unwise to be dismissive of President Trump.” On Thursday, Loomer put her podcast on hiatus, saying she had been "running on empty for too long" and needed to focus on her personal life and upcoming wedding. She’ll return in January, she added. BROKEN PROMISES The midterms also tested the beliefs that have held MAGA together, and some of them are giving way. The Democratic sweep dealt a significant setback ‌to the election denial movement, a central pillar of MAGA politics since Trump's 2020 defeat. Candidates who embraced his false claims of widespread voter fraud lost heavily, including several who had ​worked to overturn the 2020 result. Election deniers will hold at least 41 fewer congressional and statewide offices next year, and they have lost ​70% of the called races for statewide posts that oversee elections, according to States United Action, a nonprofit that tracks such candidates. Trump made no effort to contest the results and instead blamed Republicans for the defeat. With few close races and no credible basis for a challenge, many prominent pro-Trump election skeptics dropped fraud allegations and urged supporters to keep organizing. A handful of allies still alleged, without evidence, that the vote was rigged. Mike Lindell, the MyPillow founder and promoter of false claims that machines flipped votes in 2020, said he was not concerned by Trump's pledge to accept the results. “That's his opinion. I've got a different opinion,” Lindell told Reuters. “I think it's all been stolen.” But such claims stayed largely on the fringe, even among Republicans. Without contested races, the MAGA election denial movement risks losing the money, attention and momentum that sustained it. "Nobody's going to be putting money behind it," said Wendy Via, co-founder of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism, a nonprofit that tracks ​hate speech and extremism. Retired Lieutenant General Mike Flynn, who falsely claimed the 2020 election was stolen and is a popular figure in the Christian nationalist wing of the MAGA movement, accepted the defeat. He ‌called the results “a massacre” and criticized Trump and his administration for failing to deliver on pledges ranging from lowering costs to releasing the government’s investigative files on Epstein. Responding to Vice President JD Vance’s assessment on X that the Iran war was “the reason we lost,” Flynn wrote: “the sheer number of broken promises is why the blue tsunami happened." Flynn also criticized Christian voters for failing to show up. “As a Catholic and a Christian, I’m sorely embarrassed and disappointed,” he ​wrote. Other prominent Christian nationalists were divided over whether MAGA can outlast Trump. Douglas Wilson, a Christian nationalist pastor who was invited by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to deliver a sermon at the Pentagon in February, told Reuters that MAGA “is not going anywhere” but must become less personality-driven and more focused on border control, tax cuts and avoiding foreign wars. Joel Webbon, a far-right Christian nationalist pastor from Texas, was far less sanguine. “Trump lost this all by himself,” ​he said in a video on X, arguing that the president abandoned his base by embracing Israel, launching the war in Iran and failing to follow through on releasing the Epstein files and mass deportations. “MAGA is dead,” Webbon wrote in an accompanying post. “Forever.” (Editing by Jason Szep) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-cost-us-midterm-losses-110625474.html

item.title: Immigration crackdown isn't expected to ease after GOP election losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Trump administration is unlikely to scale back its aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration following the results of the midterm elections , multiple U.S. officials told CBS News, citing the elevation of immigration hawk Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff. Republicans suffered huge losses across the country on Election Day, including in some historically red states like Texas . Exit polls indicated that immigration was one of the top issues, alongside the economy, among Texas Latinos, who swung heavily toward Democrats. And 58% of voters nationwide said the Trump administration's deportation crackdown had "gone too far." In January, Democratic lawmakers will take control of both chambers of Congress and assume sweeping powers to investigate the administration's immigration crackdown and its most controversial policies. Still, officials at the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement have not received instructions to reduce immigration enforcement since the election, the sources said, requesting anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media. In recent weeks, ICE officials have been instructed to try to carry out around 19,000 arrests per week, or about 2,700 per day, an increase from a prior 2,000 daily arrest target, agency sources told CBS News. That target was set before the midterms. The U.S. officials cited Miller's appointment to the top post in the White House as a clear indication the Trump administration is likely to continue ICE's deportation blitz, as well as its quieter yet far-reaching campaign to sharply restrict legal immigration. Asked if the midterms would usher in a pullback in immigration enforcement, one of the officials responded, "I would count on the opposite" with Miller as chief of staff. The sources also said the administration believes the stunning electoral losses last week were largely driven by concerns about the economy, affordability and the war with Iran — not its immigration crackdown. "This administration will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens who terrorize our communities. There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CBS News. Bis cited the Trump administration's efforts to bolster security at the U.S.-Mexico border, where illegal crossings have plunged to historically low levels after soaring to record highs under former President Joe Biden's tenure. In a statement Sunday, DHS said ICE would not be "backing away or slowing down." "Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS will continue to enforce our nation's laws and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets," DHS added. Miller has been seen as a loyal foot soldier in Mr. Trump's inner circle for a decade, since his successful 2016 presidential campaign, when he promised to shut down Muslim immigration to the U.S. and dramatically expand deportations of those in the U.S. illegally. During that time, Miller has solidified himself as the chief architect of Mr. Trump's hardline immigration policies. Miller was one of Mr. Trump's top aides during his first administration, when officials banned immigration and travel from Muslim-majority countries and separated thousands of migrant children from their parents as part of a "zero tolerance" crackdown that was abandoned after massive public uproar. But Miller has greatly expanded his power — and his influence over federal immigration policymaking — since Mr. Trump's return to the White House. In less than two years, with Miller as deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, the second Trump administration has effectively closed the U.S. asylum system; shut down refugee admissions, with a notable exemption for White South Africans; tightened access to different legal immigration benefits like green cards; and undertaken highly visible ICE and Border Patrol arrest operations across the country. Those immigration enforcement operations have often triggered widespread community backlash, including in January, when federal immigration officials killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti , during a crackdown in Minneapolis that the administration scaled back following bipartisan outcry. Miller has publicly floated the idea of suspending habeas corpus — the conditional right for people to challenge unlawful detention — for ICE detainees. Habeas cases have skyrocketed over the past two years, as the Trump administration has greatly narrowed other avenues for those fighting deportation to be released from ICE detention. In addition to his immigration portfolio, Miller has also played an influential role in the Trump administration's crackdown on universities and legal groups, and its campaign to investigate allegations of fraud in Democratic-led states like Minnesota. Theresa Cardinal Brown, an immigration official at DHS during the Obama and Bush administrations, said the Trump administration's deportation efforts are likely to face some obstacles next year. She expects congressional Democrats to use their new powers to try to rein in ICE, including by issuing a flurry of subpoenas, holding oversight hearings and passing measures to limit immigration enforcement funds. Cardinal Brown also predicts that some communities and states with newly elected Democratic leaders, like Texas, may scrap or limit policies that allowed or required local law enforcement officials to work with ICE. Last week, Houston's mayor said he would direct local police to limit their cooperation with ICE, following the election results. But Cardinal Brown stressed that Mr. Trump will likely veto any Democratic attempts to restrict ICE enforcement and noted the agency received $75 billion in funds through 2029 due to the "One Big Beautiful Bill" that the president signed into law last year. "They're going to continue apace," Cardinal Brown said. "They have the money. They have the resources." item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Newly appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and the Department of Justice have reportedly been considering throwing journalists in jail to get them to reveal their sources when government intel is leaked, according to a report. Following Susie Wiles’ exit as chief of staff, The Atlantic reported that President Donald Trump urged the DOJ to pursue criminal-leak investigations on national security grounds. There have reportedly been discussions among White House officials about tactics they could use to get journalists to reveal their sources — including arresting them, three people familiar with the subject told the outlet. Two people described Wiles pushing back against trying to force journalists to divulge their government sources, while Miller was in favor of the move, insisting that it wouldn’t take long for journalists to give up their sources, according to the report. A DOJ spokesperson told The Atlantic : “This is absolutely false,” and reiterated that when approached for comment by The Independent. The new White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller is reportedly on board with jailing journalists to get them to reveal their sources, according to a report (Reuters) Meanwhile, a White House spokesperson told The Independent: “Unauthorized leaks of sensitive national security information will NEVER be tolerated. They endanger American lives and threaten our national security. Those responsible must be held accountable.” It is not illegal for journalists to receive — and write about — classified information they have received from a government leaker, even if the source themselves has violated the law by sharing the information. In 1971, The New York Times published excerpts of a leaked report detailing the U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War, prompting the Nixon administration to try and block the publication of the leaked files. However, the Supreme Court ruled in favor of the newspaper and press freedom. On Friday, Trump revealed that his longtime aide, Miller, would be replacing Wiles, who Trump was reportedly “furious” with after Republicans lost control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections. A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a time when the Republican Party's midterm defeat could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda. Wiles is moving to Trump’s political operation as Stephen Miller takes over her job as White House Chief of Staff (Getty) However, he is best known for driving Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, which has been widely unpopular among Americans. Just 36% of respondents to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed early this week approve of Trump’s mass deportation agenda, with 54% disapproving. Still, Trump announced Miller as Wiles’ replacement on Friday. “I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. item.title: Netanyahu rival Eisenkot seeks 'wide' government, but his path to power is uncertain
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Steven Scheer JERUSALEM, Nov 8 (Reuters) - Former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot said on Sunday he will work to form a wide government as quickly as possible, but his path to power was uncertain following a deadlocked election that failed to dislodge Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Israeli ‌President Isaac Herzog on Saturday gave Eisenkot the first opportunity to try to form a new government after the October 27 election left both Eisenkot ‌and Netanyahu short of the majority needed to govern. Herzog officially handed Eisenkot the task on Sunday at a meeting at the president's residence, starting the clock on what Eisenkot said would be an "extraordinarily complex" ​process. "We are in a state of emergency, approaching a point of no return for the State of Israel," Eisenkot said. "We must form a national emergency government. This will require creative and unconventional political steps." Eisenkot said Israeli democracy was at a vulnerable moment at a time when it faced immense challenges, with Herzog citing a threat of attack from Iran, the need to progress towards peace in Gaza and negotiations with Lebanon and other neighbours. "There is great urgency for new leadership, leadership that people can look in the eye ‌and trust," Eisenkot said. His potential pathways to power include trying ⁠to form a minority government with Arab party support for key issues; forming a coalition with ultra-Orthodox parties that he and his allies have shunned in the past; or forging a unity government with Netanyahu. All three options face formidable obstacles. NEGOTIATIONS COULD TAKE ⁠SIX WEEKS Eisenkot said he will call on all parties to join who meet his main principles. These include recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; a duty of national service for all to strengthen the military and expand its ranks; and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization and a commitment to destroying its military and governing capacity. "I am ​convinced ​that it is possible and right to form a new government quickly, one that will win ​a large majority in the Knesset," Eisenkot said, referring to Israel's ‌parliament. Eisenkot now has 28 days plus a possible 14-day extension. If he fails, Netanyahu will likely get his shot at forming a government. Should he also be unable, new elections could be called. Herzog, who consulted with all parties, said Eisenkot received the "clear and unequivocal support" of a majority of lawmakers on who has the better chance of forming the next government that will win the confidence of the Knesset. Netanyahu's Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but Netanyahu's wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total, short of a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat parliament. Eisenkot's Yashar party emerged as the second-largest party with 21 ‌seats, while his coalition, spanning four centre-left to right-wing Jewish-led parties, won just 48 seats. Two ​parties representing Israel's Arab minority won an unprecedented 19 seats. LIEBERMAN SAYS HE COULD WORK WITH ​ULTRA-ORTHODOX PARTIES Netanyahu called for a unity government of all Zionist parties to preserve ​a Jewish state, while giving no indication whether he would was prepared to serve under Eisekenkot's leadership. "This is the will of the ‌people and the need of the hour," he said in ​a statement, ruling out a coalition government with Arabs - ​who make up 21% of Israel's population. Potentially making Eisenkot's job tougher is the position of one opposition leader, Avigdor Lieberman of the Israel Our Home party, who has ruled out a unity government with Netanyahu or a minority government that has backing from Arab parties. But Lieberman has softened his stance ​on sitting with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties as long as they ‌agree to support a law under which ultra-Orthodox men serve in the military. "Given the current reality, in order to prevent further elections and bring ​an end to the Netanyahu era, there is no choice but to make difficult decisions and resolve issues where flexibility is possible and ​common ground can be found," Lieberman said. (Reporting by Steven Scheer; editing by Philippa Fletcher) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/netanyahu-rival-eisenkot-seeks-wide-173553169.html

item.title: U.S. forces are ready to strike Iran, but Trump doubts they'll need to
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
US President Donald Trump looks on at a midterm campaign rally at Five Flags Center in Dubuque, Iowa on November 1, 2026. - Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images President Donald Trump said on Sunday that it is “highly unlikely” he will need to order the US back to war with Iran as long as there is progress in negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear program and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, repeating his assertion five times during an interview with CNN. “It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump told CNN’s Jim Sciutto during a 20-minute phone interview, referring to Iran. “The answer is highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary. They’re a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation. Highly unlikely it will be necessary. I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them.” “So it’s highly unlikely I’ll have to,” he continued. “They’re withering away financially. We’ve hit them militarily. We could finish them off.” ‘We’re ready for it’ Eight months after the war started, the two sides have been in a stalemate, with little military action or significant diplomatic progress made while oil tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz have come under Iranian attack. The two countries and officials from Qatar, which has mediated the talks, have kept quiet about the status of their negotiations. But Iranian hardliners have seized on the results of last week’s midterm elections — fueled in part by the war’s unpopularity with US voters — as a sign of a weakened Trump presidency that would be more willing to given in to their country’s demands to be allowed to continue its nuclear program, which it says it needs for energy, and maintain control of the strait. Iran has also struggled to sell crude oil on global markets under US sanctions, while billions of dollars in assets held in foreign banks have been frozen. Trump, who has in the past offered mixed messages about his willingness to end the war, made clear during the interview that US forces are in position in the region if he were to give the order to strike. “We’re ready for it. I’ve got three aircraft carriers here. The other one just arrived. We have three. They’re fully locked and loaded,” he said. The president also said that the US has identified infrastructure targets inside Iran in the event of renewed military action, including power plants and bridges. “We have 38 bridges in our site that we can knock down in literally one hour, “ he said. “They’ll all be down.” However, he said he would prefer not to destroy Iranian infrastructure. “I don’t want to do that because essentially, it’ll take 10 years to rebuild them,” he said. “I don’t like ripping down bridges. And the hardest thing to build is a bridge. It takes years, and I’m a good builder.” Diplomatic activity across the Middle East has increased since Tuesday’s midterm elections. On Friday, Qatar said that Trump had called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss de-escalation, and a day earlier, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke with his counterparts from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Pakistan, Kuwait, Jordan, Turkey, Cyprus and Qatar. Depleted Iranian stockpiles In terms of Iran’s ability to defend against new US strikes, Trump said Iran’s air defenses have been destroyed. “It’s unstoppable because they have no anti-aircraft stuff. All of their anti-aircraft is gone,” he said. The president also provided new details on the state of Iranian missile and drone stockpiles, saying that the regime maintains 10% of its missile capacity and 15% of its drone capabilities. “The only thing they can do is about 10% level — make some missiles and make some drones. Drones at about 15% because much of their factories are gone,” he said. “Most likely it will not be necessary,” he repeated about the prospect of new military action. “They want to make a deal so badly.” CNN’s Mostafa Salem contributed to this story. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) on Sunday warned that Democrats could investigate everything from pardons Trump made earlier in his second term to Trump allies including Elon Musk and the president’s newly appointed chief of staff Stephen Miller. Still, Sanders on Sunday said the election was about more than just Americans wanting to tackle the Trump administration’s “corruption and illegal, unconstitutional actions.” “What I think this election was about, is the American people not only expressing disgust with Trump and his policies, but are demanding real change, no more tinkering around the edges,” said Sanders. “And what the American people are saying: Look, we are working long hours. We're worried about our kids. We can't afford healthcare. We can't afford housing.” But Sanders, who serves on the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) , also told CNN’s “State of the Union” that he would be “open” to a proposal by Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.) to impeach Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. item.title: Doctor having lunch near Krakow shooting likely saved officer's life, colleague says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
[Getty Images] One of two surgeons who treated victims on the streets in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland said his colleague"undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer. The pair were eating near the city's Main Market Square on Saturday when a gunman began firing at random, killing six and injuring 15. The doctors raced to treat both the attacker and two officers shot while subduing the perpetrator. On Sunday, the officers - both hailed as "true heroes" by the prime minister for preventing further deaths - emerged from comas. Prosecutors launched a terror investigation after ministers previously said the 24-year-old Polish attacker - who remains in a critical condition - was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies". A British national and Austrian woman were among those killed alongside four Poles. Professor Michal Pędziwiatr and Dr Mateusz Wierdak were having lunch in central Krakow with their families when they heard gunshots, local media reported. "Suddenly my son ran up and said: 'Dad, they're shooting at people there, people are falling to the ground'," Pędziwiatr told news outlet Fakt. Pędziwiatr said when they got to the scene, they treated both the apparent attacker and the police officers. "When it comes to saving lives, it doesn't matter who is who," he added. Once the shooting stopped, Pędziwiatr said he took care of the other victims and the perpetrator, while Wierdak began working on the police officer who was shot in the chest during the gunfight. Watch: Professor Michal Pędziwiatr says Dr Mateusz Wierdak is "a hero" "He, to put it colloquially, stuffed all the bandages into [the police officer's] chest and stuck his hands in," he told Fakt. "If not for that, I don't know how things would have turned out, as there was a long wait for the ambulance." Meanwhile, Pędziwiatr said he called John Paul II Hospital where the Department of Thoracic and Cardiac Surgery is located. "I insisted they take him there because, in my opinion, he had the best chance of survival there, where there were specialists for precisely this type of injury," he told Fakt. According to local media, Wierdak is a renowned surgeon in Krakow. The University Hospital in Krakow states Pędziwiatr is head of General, Oncological, Metabolic and Emergency Surgery. The police officers have been identified as senior constables Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański. Investigations continued in central Krakow on Sunday before Main Market Square reopened [Reuters] The attacker has not yet been named by authorities. When his house was searched after the attack in central Krakow, the bodies of his parents and sister were found. The National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland launched an investigation into the attack with a unit specialising in "terrorist offences" taking the lead. Separately, reports emerged that six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers also assisted in the aftermath of the shooting. James McConnell, an officer, told RTE News the group were on a city break and were close to the main square when the shooting happened. The volunteers who are trained to provide medical care immediately sought to help injured people, providing "CPR and haemorrhage control". Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded. Ruby Catherine Warren, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives". Not knowing where the gunman was - or if there was more than one - they "just kept sprinting", eventually finding a hotel to hide inside. Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover". "I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away," he said. The suspect wore full military tactical gear during the attack and was described as having a military-grade weapon - but the government said he was not a member of the Polish armed forces. Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said "everything suggests" the suspect was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held ultra-nationalist views. The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) on Saturday in the historic centre of Krakow. Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out. The glass fronts of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes. The mayor of Krakow said he had submitted an urgent request for the two officers injured while stopping the attacker to be awarded titles of honorary citizens of the city. Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted. item.title: El-Sayed says he is 'happy' to work with Trump on Medicare for all and other priorities
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday opened the door to potentially working with President Donald Trump to pass legislation securing nationwide affordable healthcare. In an interview with ABC’s “This Week,” the progressive from Michigan called Trump an “unserious fool” but said he would be “happy” to sit down with the president to discuss how best to serve Michiganders. “Look, I've never met the man. I am — he is the president of the United States. I am the U.S. senator-elect from the state of Michigan. I am happy to meet with him like I'll meet with anyone who can advance the goals I ran on: to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for All,” El-Sayed said. “I've said this, if he wants to pass Trump Care for All, which will guarantee health care to everyone and put his name on it like he's putting his name on everything, I'm game. Let's see if he wants to do that.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump was vociferous in his criticism of El-Sayed throughout the campaign season, lambasting El-Sayed for his progressive policies and repeatedly mocking his name. Trump had supported former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in the bitter Michigan race. El-Sayed on Sunday said he is not aware of any attempts at communication from Rogers. "I think he has a flight to catch to Florida," El-Sayed quipped. Though born and raised in Michigan, Rogers moved to Florida with his wife after leaving Congress in 2015. (Rogers' campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) Despite his apparent openness to meet with Trump, El-Sayed criticized the president for appointing Stephen Miller to be the White House’s new chief of staff — evidence, El-Sayed argued, of Trump’s lack of seriousness when Americans are demanding affordability and accountability. “So, look, if he wants to act serious, we are happy to work alongside him to actually address these issues," he said. "He is the president of the United States, but he wants to continue to fool he will hire people like Stephen Miller to run the White House. And he gets to choose where he goes next."
